# Submission note — parsimagma refuter

**Compressed data or binary blobs:** none. The solver is plain Python with no
embedded payload; the construction corpus is regenerated by a loop at runtime.

**Sources drawn on:** no Contributor Network item. The ordering in `PRIORITY`
comes from my own prior open-source work,
<https://github.com/carlok/parsimagma> (Apache-2.0), described under
"Reproducing the ordering" below. Nothing else.

## What it does

One strategy, applied to every problem: enumerate small **linear and affine
magmas** `x ◇ y = a·x + b·y + c` over `Z/m`, keep the first that satisfies the
hypothesis and violates the goal, and certify it with plain `decide`.

No LLM calls. No embedded data — the corpus is regenerated by a loop, so this
solver is code all the way down and the size is ~9 KB.

## Why a linear sweep is the right first move

Measured over the Equational Theories Project's own implication graph, on the
13,855,357 implications it records as false:

| instances | false implications refuted | share |
|---|---|---|
| 4 (the whole of `Z/2`) | 11,871,871 | 85.7% |
| 25 | 13,472,458 | 97.2% |
| 2,786 (full corpus) | 13,834,667 | 99.85% |

The ordering in `PRIORITY` is the prefix of a greedy set cover computed against
that graph, which is why `Z/2` comes first and why most problems finish in
milliseconds. On 400 uniformly sampled false order-≤4 implications the search
refutes 385 (96.2%), and 342 of those are settled by a two-element magma.

The tail is long but generated, not stored: `x ◇ y = 7x + 7y` over `Z/13` alone
refutes 268 of the 1062 implications Vampire left undecided in
[Janota, arXiv:2508.15856] — instances no search-based finite model builder
tried (Vampire `fmb`, Mace4, z3 on a ground encoding) reaches at all.

## Reproducing the ordering

The corpus, the coverage figures and the greedy cover are in
<https://github.com/carlok/parsimagma> (Apache-2.0), which computes signatures
for ~2,786 constructions over the 4694-law set and reports coverage against the
ETP graph. `PRIORITY` in the solver is the first twenty rows of the greedy cover
over false implications. Everything else in the solver is a plain loop over
`(m, a, b, c)`, so no part of it needs the repository to run.

## Measured on the stress test

Against the 200-problem `stage2_stress_test` set, which mirrors the graded
distribution:

| category | false | true |
|---|---|---|
| order4_normal | 23/25 | 0/25 |
| order4_hard | 17/25 | 0/25 |
| order4_extra_hard | 0/25 | 0/25 |
| order5_normal | 15/25 | 0/25 |
| **total** | **55/100** | **0/100** |

**55/200.** Two things that number makes plain. The `extra_hard` category is
selected against exactly this method and the corpus reaches none of it, so the
96.2% quoted above — which is over *uniformly sampled* false implications from
the ETP graph — does not transfer to a curated set. And the solver takes a zero
on all 100 true implications by design.

## Scope, stated plainly

This solver **refutes**; it does not prove. The only true-implication case it
attempts is the degenerate one where the hypothesis collapses the carrier to a
point. It answers nothing on the rest and takes the zero, which the scoring
rules make costless.

## Implementation notes

- The operation is emitted as a Lean function, not through `finOpTable`. That
  helper reads its argument one character at a time, so a table entry of ten or
  more is silently split in two and every carrier above 9 is wrong. A rule also
  states in a few dozen bytes against the 20,000-byte certificate cap.
- Candidates are skipped when `carrier^arity` exceeds a cap, since the problem
  set contains six-variable laws where a naive sweep does not terminate.
- Certificates depend on `propext` alone; `native_decide` is not used anywhere.
